title: Running totals, frames, moving averages, top-N per group
summary: The frame is the part of the partition an aggregate or last_value reads. With ORDER BY it defaults to "start through the current row's last peer", which gives running totals; ROWS counts rows, RANGE measures distance on the value. Top-N per group is row_number or rank in a subquery.

examples.title: Running totals: the default RANGE frame, ROWS, and the last_value trap

annotations.note: With an ORDER BY the default frame is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, and in RANGE mode CURRENT ROW means the current row's last peer. Runs 2 and 3 share 11-10, so each frame contains both: 8 and 8, never the 4 in between.

ROWS ends the frame at the row itself, so the total climbs one run at a time: 3, 4, 8, 10. ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING is short for BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW. id makes the order unique; the docs warn that ROWS gives unpredictable results when it isn't.
No ORDER BY: every row is a peer of every other, the frame is the whole partition, and sum is the project total.

first_value, last_value and nth_value read the frame, not the partition. The default frame stops at the current row (its last peer, and the order here is unique), so last_value returns the row's own value. The docs call this result unhelpful.

A frame over the whole partition makes last_value the latest run's count: 2 for TraceLite on every row. first_value(failed) OVER (PARTITION BY project ORDER BY ran_on DESC, id DESC) gives the same answer with the default frame.

examples.title: Moving averages: last three builds (ROWS) vs last three days (RANGE)

annotations.note: ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW: this build and the two rows before it, whatever their dates. At the start of the data the frame is shorter, so the first two averages cover one and two builds; n_builds makes that visible.
RANGE with an offset (PG 11) measures distance on the ORDER BY value: rows dated at most 2 days before this one. For a date or timestamp column the offset is an interval.
They agree until the weekend gap. On 11-09 the three-build window reaches back to Thursday's 30-minute outlier and reports 19.0; the three-day window finds only Monday itself and reports 14.0.

Both ends of a frame may precede the current row: the three builds before this one. Leaving the row out keeps a spike from raising its own baseline, so 30 minutes is compared with 11.0 and flagged. The first build has an empty frame, avg over no rows is NULL, and so is spike.

SQLSTATE 42P20. A RANGE offset is a distance between the current row's value and other rows' values, which only makes sense for a single sort key. ROWS and GROUPS offsets count rows and peer groups and have no such restriction.

examples.title: Top-N per group with row_number and rank, and the run condition in the plan

annotations.note: The tutorial's own pattern: number the rows of each partition in a subquery, keep rn <= 2 outside. With a unique order every suite gets at most two rows; search has only one test and returns one.

rank answers "top 2 including ties": Giriş and Çıkış share second place, so auth returns three rows. dense_rank() <= 2 would mean "every test with one of the two slowest durations", which can be many more.
The tied rows need an order for display; COLLATE "tr-x-icu" puts Çıkış before Giriş as the Turkish alphabet does.

Run Condition (PG 15): rn <= 2 moved into the WindowAgg, and the Subquery Scan has no Filter left. The Window line says ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING although the query never did: row_number ignores the frame, so the planner uses the cheaper ROWS mode (PG 16). It lists the order columns without direction; the DESC is in the Sort Key.
SQLSTATE 42703. An output column's name can be used in ORDER BY and GROUP BY but not in WHERE or HAVING, and here the value doesn't even exist when WHERE runs. Hence the subquery.

use_cases: Running totals and cumulative counts: failures to date, burn-down charts, account balances
Moving averages that smooth noisy series: build times, response times, daily sign-ups over the last 7 days
Baselines for anomaly detection: compare each value with the average of the N values before it
Top-N per group: the 3 slowest tests per suite, the latest 5 runs per test case, best sellers per category
A partition's first or last value next to every row: the latest status shown on each historic run
strengths: One sorted pass computes running and moving aggregates; the correlated-subquery version re-reads earlier rows for every row
sum, count and avg have an inverse transition function, so a sliding frame subtracts the row that leaves instead of recomputing (the docs' moving-aggregate mode)
RANGE with an interval follows the calendar, so missing days shrink the frame instead of silently stretching it as a fixed row count does
row_number top-N is standard SQL and works for any N, which DISTINCT ON (N = 1 only) can't; rank and dense_rank make tie handling explicit
weaknesses: The default frame surprises: adding ORDER BY turns a total into a running total and last_value into 'this row', with no error
ROWS frames over a non-unique ORDER BY give unpredictable results, while RANGE treats peers alike but measures values, not rows
Top-N with row_number still sorts every row of every partition; with few groups and an index on (group, sort key), LATERAL ... LIMIT N reads only N index entries per group
RANGE offsets need exactly one ORDER BY column, of a type with distance arithmetic such as numbers, dates or timestamps

pitfalls.title: Running total over a non-unique order
pitfalls.detail: With the default RANGE frame, all rows of one day show the day's final total. If each row should add its own amount, make the order unique and use ROWS.
pitfalls.bad: sum(failed) OVER (PARTITION BY project ORDER BY ran_on)
pitfalls.good: sum(failed) OVER (PARTITION BY project ORDER BY ran_on, id ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING)

pitfalls.title: last_value with the default frame
pitfalls.detail: The frame ends at the current row, so last_value returns the current row's value. Widen the frame, or flip the order and use first_value.
pitfalls.bad: last_value(status) OVER (PARTITION BY test_case ORDER BY ran_at)
pitfalls.good: first_value(status) OVER (PARTITION BY test_case ORDER BY ran_at DESC, id DESC)

pitfalls.title: 'Last 7 days' written as ROWS
pitfalls.detail: ROWS counts rows. When days are missing, six preceding rows reach further back than a week. Use RANGE with an interval, or fill the gaps with generate_series first if a missing day should count as zero.
pitfalls.bad: avg(minutes) OVER (ORDER BY built_on ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
pitfalls.good: avg(minutes) OVER (ORDER BY built_on RANGE BETWEEN '6 days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)

pitfalls.title: Partial frames at the start of the data
pitfalls.detail: The first rows of a moving average average fewer values than the window size, without any marker. Return count(*) over the same frame, and hide or flag rows below the full size.

pitfalls.title: Top-N with row_number when ties matter
pitfalls.detail: row_number <= 3 cuts a tie for third place arbitrarily. If tied rows should all appear, use rank() <= 3 and accept more than three rows.

quiz.q: Two runs share ran_on = 11-10. What does `sum(failed) OVER (ORDER BY ran_on)` show on them?
options: The same total, which includes both runs
quiz.why: The default frame is RANGE ... CURRENT ROW, which ends at the last peer, so both rows' frames contain both runs.

quiz.q: Builds on Thursday, Friday and Monday, none at the weekend. On Monday, which rows does `ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` include?
options: Monday and the two builds before it, Thursday and Friday
quiz.why: ROWS counts rows regardless of their dates. RANGE BETWEEN '2 days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW would include only Monday.

quiz.q: You need the 3 slowest tests per suite, and every test tied for third place must be included. Which filter?
quiz.why: rank gives tied rows the same position (1, 2, 3, 3), so all of them pass <= 3. row_number cuts the tie arbitrarily; dense_rank <= 3 returns every test with one of the three slowest durations.

quiz.q: Why does `last_value(x) OVER (PARTITION BY p ORDER BY t)` return the current row's x?
options: The default frame ends at the current row's last peer
last_value only works with ROWS mode
quiz.why: last_value reads the last row of the frame, and the default frame with ORDER BY stops at the current row's peer group.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: Window Function Calls (frame clause)
PostgreSQL docs: Window Functions (first_value, last_value and frames)

body:
## Concept

Inside its partition, every window call has a **frame**: the rows that an aggregate, or
`first_value`, `last_value` and `nth_value`, read for the current row. Ranking functions
and `lag`/`lead` ignore the frame and work on the whole partition.

A frame clause has a mode and two ends:
`{ ROWS | RANGE | GROUPS } BETWEEN start AND end`, where each end is
`UNBOUNDED PRECEDING`, `n PRECEDING`, `CURRENT ROW`, `n FOLLOWING` or
`UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING`.

- **ROWS:** `n` counts rows, and `CURRENT ROW` is the row itself.
- **RANGE:** `n` is a distance on the single `ORDER BY` value: a number, or an
  `interval` for dates and timestamps (offsets since PG 11). `CURRENT ROW` includes all
  peers of the row.
- **GROUPS** (PG 11): `n` counts peer groups, sets of rows equal in the `ORDER BY`.

Without a frame clause: no `ORDER BY` means the whole partition; with `ORDER BY` it is
`RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`, from the start through the current
row's last peer. That default is why `sum(...) OVER (ORDER BY ...)` is a running total.

**Top-N per group** doesn't need frames: number each partition with `row_number()` (or
`rank()`, to keep ties) in a subquery and keep the rows numbered up to N.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **pandas:** `groupby(...).cumsum()` is a `ROWS` running total, where ties don't share
  a value. `rolling(3).mean()` is `ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`, except
  that pandas returns NaN until three values exist, while SQL averages whatever the
  frame holds. `rolling('3D')` on a datetime index is the `RANGE` version.
  `sort_values(...).groupby(...).head(2)` is top-N.
- **C/C++, Java, Go:** a running total is an accumulator in a loop. A `ROWS` moving
  average is a ring buffer of the last N values; a `RANGE` frame is the two-pointer
  sliding window, dropping old elements while they are more than the offset behind the
  current one.
- **Everyone:** the frame is per row. Each row gets its own slice of the partition, so
  one `SELECT` can report a running total, a moving average and a whole-partition value
  side by side.

## How it works

The `WindowAgg` node walks the sorted partition and keeps each frame's aggregate state.
When the frame's start moves forward (`2 PRECEDING`), aggregates with an inverse
transition function, such as `sum` and `count`, subtract the row that left instead of
recomputing; the docs call it moving-aggregate mode, and it makes the cost proportional
to the number of rows rather than rows times frame length.

Top-N has a planner optimization of its own. Since PostgreSQL 15 a filter such as
`rn <= 2` over `row_number()`, `rank()`, `dense_rank()` or `count()` becomes a **run
condition** of the `WindowAgg` (example 3's plan); PostgreSQL 16 added `ntile()`,
`cume_dist()` and `percent_rank()` (both versions' release notes). These values only grow
within a partition (`count()` when its frame starts at the partition's first row, as by
default), so once the condition fails no later row of that partition can pass. Per the
executor's source (src/backend/executor/nodeWindowAgg.c, function ExecWindowAgg), the
node then stops computing them: without `PARTITION BY` (and no other window above it) it
stops reading altogether; with one it still reads the rest of each partition, skipping
the window functions, and any Sort below has sorted every row anyway. On PostgreSQL 18.7 over 1,000,000 rows,
`EXPLAIN ANALYZE` showed the Seq Scan under `row_number() OVER ()` with `rn <= 2`
returning 3 rows; with `PARTITION BY` it returned all 1,000,000.

## Design notes

Write the frame clause explicitly whenever an aggregate's window has an `ORDER BY`. The
default is right for a running total over a unique order and surprising everywhere
else; an explicit `ROWS` or `RANGE` tells the next reader which one you meant.

For time series, decide what a missing period means. If no build means "no data", use
`RANGE` with an interval, as example 2 does. If it means zero (no sales that day),
generate the calendar with `generate_series`, `LEFT JOIN` the data to it, and then a
`ROWS` frame over complete days is correct.

For top-N per group there are three tools. `row_number()` in a subquery is portable
and works for any N; `rank()` when ties must stay. `DISTINCT ON` (the grouping-sets
lesson) is the shortest for N = 1. When groups are few and each is large, `LATERAL`
with `ORDER BY ... LIMIT N` over an index on `(group, sort key)` reads N index entries
per group instead of sorting everything (the LATERAL lesson).

files.examples/01_running_totals.sql:
-- LEARN(sql.windows.frames): the frame decides which rows an aggregate OVER (...) sees.
CREATE TABLE runs (
  id      int  PRIMARY KEY,
  project text NOT NULL,
  ran_on  date NOT NULL,
  failed  int  NOT NULL          -- failed tests in this run
);
INSERT INTO runs VALUES
  (1, 'TraceLite', '2026-11-09', 3),
  (2, 'TraceLite', '2026-11-10', 1),
  (3, 'TraceLite', '2026-11-10', 4),   -- a second run on the same day
  (4, 'TraceLite', '2026-11-12', 2),
  (5, 'StackLab',  '2026-11-10', 5),
  (6, 'StackLab',  '2026-11-11', 0);

-- ORDER BY inside OVER turns sum into a running sum. The default frame
-- (RANGE) ends at the current row's last peer; ROWS ends at the row itself.
SELECT project, ran_on, id, failed,
       sum(failed) OVER (PARTITION BY project ORDER BY ran_on) AS range_default,
       sum(failed) OVER (PARTITION BY project ORDER BY ran_on, id
                         ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING)             AS rows_running,
       sum(failed) OVER (PARTITION BY project)                 AS project_total
FROM runs
ORDER BY project, ran_on, id;

-- last_value sees the frame, not the partition: with the default frame the
-- "last" row is the current one. Widen the frame to get the latest run.
SELECT project, id, failed,
       last_value(failed) OVER (PARTITION BY project ORDER BY ran_on, id)
         AS last_default,
       last_value(failed) OVER (PARTITION BY project ORDER BY ran_on, id
                                ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING
                                         AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING)
         AS latest_failed
FROM runs
ORDER BY project, id;
files.examples/02_moving_average.sql:
CREATE TABLE nightly_builds (
  built_on date PRIMARY KEY,
  minutes  int  NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO nightly_builds VALUES
  ('2026-11-02', 10), ('2026-11-03', 12), ('2026-11-04', 11),
  ('2026-11-05', 30), ('2026-11-06', 13),
  -- no builds on the weekend of 11-07 and 11-08
  ('2026-11-09', 14), ('2026-11-10', 12);

-- "Last three builds" (ROWS) vs "last three days" (RANGE with an interval).
-- count(*) over the same frame shows how many rows each average used.
SELECT built_on, minutes,
       round(avg(minutes) OVER last3_rows, 1) AS avg_3_builds,
       count(*)           OVER last3_rows     AS n_builds,
       round(avg(minutes) OVER last3_days, 1) AS avg_3_days,
       count(*)           OVER last3_days     AS n_days
FROM nightly_builds
WINDOW last3_rows AS (ORDER BY built_on ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW),
       last3_days AS (ORDER BY built_on
                      RANGE BETWEEN '2 days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
ORDER BY built_on;

-- A baseline that excludes the current row: the three builds before it.
SELECT built_on, minutes, baseline,
       minutes > 2 * baseline AS spike
FROM (
  SELECT built_on, minutes,
         round(avg(minutes) OVER (ORDER BY built_on
                                  ROWS BETWEEN 3 PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING), 1)
           AS baseline
  FROM nightly_builds
) AS b
ORDER BY built_on;

-- RANGE with an offset measures distance on one value, so it needs exactly
-- one ORDER BY column.
SELECT built_on,
       avg(minutes) OVER (ORDER BY built_on, minutes
                          RANGE BETWEEN '2 days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
FROM nightly_builds;
files.examples/03_top_n.sql:
CREATE TABLE test_cases (
  id          int  PRIMARY KEY,
  suite       text NOT NULL,
  title       text NOT NULL,
  duration_ms int  NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO test_cases VALUES
  (1, 'auth',   'İki adımlı doğrulama', 500),
  (2, 'auth',   'Giriş',                300),
  (3, 'auth',   'Çıkış',                300),
  (4, 'auth',   'Şifre sıfırlama',      200),
  (5, 'export', 'CSV dışa aktarım',     900),
  (6, 'export', 'PDF rapor',            400),
  (7, 'export', 'Excel',                100),
  (8, 'search', 'Arama',                 50);

-- The two slowest tests per suite: number each partition, keep 1 and 2.
SELECT suite, title, duration_ms
FROM (
  SELECT suite, title, duration_ms,
         row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY suite ORDER BY duration_ms DESC, id) AS rn
  FROM test_cases
) AS ranked
WHERE rn <= 2
ORDER BY suite, rn;

-- rank() keeps ties: auth's 2nd place is shared, so auth returns three rows.
SELECT suite, title, duration_ms, pos
FROM (
  SELECT suite, title, duration_ms,
         rank() OVER (PARTITION BY suite ORDER BY duration_ms DESC) AS pos
  FROM test_cases
) AS ranked
WHERE pos <= 2
ORDER BY suite, pos, title COLLATE "tr-x-icu";

-- The planner pushes rn <= 2 into the WindowAgg as a run condition.
ANALYZE test_cases;
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT suite, title
FROM (
  SELECT suite, title,
         row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY suite ORDER BY duration_ms DESC, id) AS rn
  FROM test_cases
) AS ranked
WHERE rn <= 2;

-- An output alias doesn't exist yet in WHERE of the same query level.
SELECT suite, title,
       row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY suite ORDER BY duration_ms DESC, id) AS rn
FROM test_cases
WHERE rn <= 2;
